query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In multi‐phase eutectic high‐entropy alloys, the accelerated degradation under simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature is primarily driven by galvanic interactions at the interphase boundaries. Wear mechanically removes the protective passive layers at these boundaries, intensifying local galvanic corrosion which in turn destabilizes the microstructure and further accelerates wear.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi‐phase eutectic high‐entropy alloy having distinct interphase boundaries with inherent differences in corrosion potential
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to simultaneous mechanical wear (e.g., sliding contact) and corrosive attack in an oxidizing environment at elevated temperature
generation.conditions: Elevated temperatures (e.g., >300°C), oxidizing medium, and controlled wear conditions that mimic sliding or abrasive contact, ensuring the phases’ galvanic interactions are active
generation.structural_mediator: Interphase boundaries acting as localized galvanic couples where differential potential drives accelerated corrosion when passive films are mechanically removed
generation.mechanism: Differential corrosion potentials between neighboring eutectic phases create galvanic cells along the interphase boundaries. Under elevated temperatures, the protective passive films on these boundaries form and then are mechanically removed by wear. This exposes fresh surfaces that rapidly corrode, compromising the local integrity of the microstructure and further enhancing mechanical degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a matched baseline (alloy with either isolated wear or corrosion exposure or a microstructure with minimized galvanic contrast), the total degradation (mass loss) will be noticeably higher. Both the individual wear rate and the corrosion rate will increase, with wear preferentially removing the degraded boundary regions and corrosion accelerating at the exposed interfaces.
generation.baseline: A comparable alloy system under either isolated wear or isolated corrosion conditions, or an alloy modified to have a more homogenized microstructure with reduced interphase potential differences
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under conditions of elevated temperature (e.g., >300°C), oxidizing environments, and mechanical wear that removes passive layers, within a eutectic microstructural framework exhibiting distinct interphase boundaries
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative enhancement in the corrosion and wear rates is uncertain, as it depends on the specific microstructural features, alloy composition, and testing conditions. Detailed parameter studies will be needed to determine the magnitude of the synergistic degradation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy eutectic alloys: one with the standard microstructure and clear interphase boundaries, and another where the interphase potential differences are minimized via a homogenization heat treatment or tailored alloying to suppress galvanic coupling. Subject both sets to simultaneous wear and corrosion testing at elevated temperature under identical conditions.
measurements: Surface and cross-sectional microstructural analysis (e.g., via SEM/EDS) to assess localized corrosion at interphase boundaries
Local corrosion potential mapping at the microstructural scale
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy with minimized interphase potential differences exhibits a degradation (total mass loss, individual wear and corrosion responses) similar to that of the standard alloy, then the hypothesis attributing accelerated coupled degradation predominantly to interphase boundary galvanic effects is falsified.
